verifications.verifierNote: The pattern is present exactly as described: src/lib/audio/wav.ts:1-3 declares SAMPLE_RATE/NUM_CHANNELS/BITS_PER_SAMPLE as module constants and :12 takes `pcm: Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>` carrying no format information. But this is the CONSUMER HALF of F081, not an independent defect: the discarded `mimeType` lives in tts.ts:27 and the only way to fix wav.ts is for tts.ts to pass the parsed format in. verifications.verifierNote: The claimed type weakness does not exist. src/lib/covers/googleBooks.ts:1 and src/lib/covers/openLibrary.ts:1 both declare `Promise<string | null>`, and that type is ACCURATE for every value either function ever resolves with: googleBooks returns `url.replace(...)` at :24 or `null` at :28; openLibrary returns a template string or `null` at :8. TypeScript's `Promise<T>` parameter describes the fulfilment value only - the language has no checked exceptions and no way to express rejection in a return type - so 'the signature lies' is a claim about a guarantee the type never made and that no TypeScript signature can make. Under this rule every fetch-calling function in every TS codebase is a finding. Verification criterion 4 also fails outright: there is no achievable replacement. The finding's own suggested fix ('catch internally and genuinely return string | null') would break the design the suite pins - src/lib/covers/index.test.ts:53-61 stubs fetch to throw and asserts `fetchCover` falls through to `placeholderCover`, which works only because the provider functions propagate. The alternative fix ('make it explicit in JSDoc') is prose, not type safety. Two further defects in the finding: the category `js-ambiguous-return` is defined by the spec as JavaScript-only and these are .ts files under `strict: true`; and the one concrete throw it names (`url.replace` on a non-string) is already counted as F085. Nothing survives that is not either inexpressible or double-counted.

The concrete failure is real: because `imageLinks` is asserted `Record<string, string>`, line 24 calls `url.replace(/^http:\/\//, 'https://')` on a value the compiler believes is a string, and `if (url)` filters falsy but not truthy-non-string, so a numeric or object value is `TypeError: url.replace is not a function`. What does not hold up is medium. verifications.verifierNote: Confirmed, and I MEASURED the finding's central claim rather than reasoning about it. tsconfig.json has `strict: true` without `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`. Running `npx tsc --noEmit --noUncheckedIndexedAccess -p tsconfig.json` produces exactly 10 errors project-wide, distributed as QuizModal.tsx 5 (78, 178, 182, 183, 232), BookDetail.tsx 3 (71, 79, 85), EReader.tsx 1 (395), AddBookModal.tsx 1 (43) - and ZERO in src/lib/goodreads.ts and ZERO in src/lib/covers/openLibrary.ts. The finding's claim that this file would compile clean under the flag is therefore true and now measured; the whole of src/lib/** is already clean. All five enumerated sites are present in current source: goodreads.ts:29 `const char = text[i]`, :33 `text[i + 1] === '"'`, :82 `(table[0] ?? [])`, :96 `(cells[index] ?? '').trim()`, and covers/openLibrary.ts:7 `data.docs?.[0]?.cover_i`. The named crash at :96 is real for a ragged row: `parseCsv` (:22-66) pushes rows of whatever length the line had, so `cells[index]` for a high index is genuinely `undefined` at runtime while the compiler insists it is `string`; only the `?? ''` prevents `TypeError: ...trim()`. The tooling note checks out too - eslint.config.js uses `tseslint.configs.recommended`, so `no-unnecessary-condition` is off and nothing will flag these guards as dead. Medium is exactly the spec's 'erodes refactor safety but isn't on a critical path'.

verifications.verifierNote: Pattern present exactly: src/lib/goodreads.ts:104 `const rating = Number.parseInt(cell(ratingAt), 10)` and :111 `rating: Number.isFinite(rating) ? rating : 0`, against `GoodreadsRow.rating: number` at :7. The finding's verified-negative is correct - `Number.isFinite` (not the coercing global `isFinite`) is used, so NaN really is killed and the NaN-propagation hypothesis does not materialise. Read sites: src/components/StatsView.tsx:20 averages into `.toFixed(1)`, src/lib/markdown.ts:14 exports `${book.rating}/5`, src/components/BookDetail.tsx:215/278/282/287, src/components/BookCard.tsx:100. verifications.verifierNote: The code defect is real and I reproduced it precisely. src/lib/srs.ts:43 applies only a floor (`Math.max(MIN_EASE, card.ease + EASE_DELTA[grade])`) with `EASE_DELTA[4] = 0.1` at :10 and no MAX_EASE anywhere in the file; :46 multiplies by `ease * INTERVAL_MODIFIER[grade]`; :52 calls `new Date(now.getTime() + intervalDays * DAY_MS).toISOString()`. Simulating consecutive grade-4 reviews reproduces the finding's numbers exactly: review 13 gives ease 3.80 / interval 94,752,480 days, review 14 gives ease 3.90 / interval 480,395,074 days and `.toISOString()` throws RangeError. `Math.max(1.3, NaN)` and `Math.max(1, NaN)` both return NaN, and `new Date(NaN).toISOString()` throws - all verified. The caller is unguarded as claimed: src/features/review/useReviewQueue.ts:38 `await cardRepo.upsert(scheduleCard(current, gradeValue))` sits in an async `useCallback` with no try/catch, and `setQueue(...)` on the next line would never run. What is wrong is the finding's assertion of 'two reachable triggers' - NEITHER is reachable. (1) Reaching review 14 requires 14 consecutive Easy grades on ONE card, and the queue is gated by `listDue` (repo.ts:84-90), which only returns cards whose `dueAt <= now`; the cumulative wall-clock wait across intervals 3, 11, 40, 151, 589, 2374, 9876, 42368, 187267, 852065, 3987664, 19180664, 94752480 days is roughly 325,000 years. `grade` also drops the card from the queue (`setQueue((rest) => rest.slice(1))`), so it cannot be re-graded within a session. (2) A non-finite `card.ease` has no producer: `reviewCards` is written only by `newCard` (ease 2.5) and `scheduleCard`, migrate.ts never touches the store, and the backup import carries only books and summaries. A latent, genuinely unreachable overflow is low, not medium.
